description: Fetch a thread by ID: headers, plaintext + HTML bodies, and attachment metadata. WHEN A THREAD IS LONG OR HTML-HEAVY, shrink the answer instead of skipping content: `bodies: "text"` drops `htmlBody` and keeps `plaintextBody` (an HTML-only mail is reduced to text and marked `bodyFromHtml: true`); `bodies: "new"` is `text` without the quoted history at the end of a reply (the trailing `>` block with its 'On ... wrote:' line, or an Outlook 'Original Message' block) and marks a cut message `quotedStripped: true` — inline answers between quoted lines, answers below a quote and forwarded messages (recognised by a forwarded-message line or a Fwd/FW/WG subject) are kept whole, except an answer below an Outlook plain-text From/Sent/Subject block, which goes with it; `bodies: "none"` drops both bodies and keeps everything else, INCLUDING the real attachment list; `lastN: 2` returns only the newest two messages, `afterMessageId` only the messages after one you have already read (both compose: after X, then the last N). The quota cost is the same whatever you keep — Gmail hands over the whole thread, these options only decide how much of it you read. `messageCount` is always the whole thread and `omittedMessages` how many the selection left out, so a partial view never passes for the whole; `bodies` is echoed when it is not `full`. `full` defaults to true and should stay true whenever content matters. `full: false` is a headers-and-labels fetch that does NOT fetch bodies or attachment metadata — the result then omits `plaintextBody`, `htmlBody` and `attachments` entirely and sets `metadataOnly: true`. `full: false` together with any `bodies` is rejected as `invalid_input` rather than silently ignored. `full: false` is kept for compatibility but DEPRECATED: use `bodies: "none"` instead, which costs the same quota and keeps the real attachment list. The fields are omitted rather than empty on purpose: an empty attachment list from a request that never looked is indistinguishable from a message that truly has none, and treating it as 'no attachment' has already nearly caused an invoice to be archived as attachment-less. If `search` reported `hasAttachments: true`, or the sender matters, use full: true (any `bodies`). EVERY MESSAGE CARRIES `authentication` — SPF/DKIM/DMARC as the RECEIVING server reported them, for answering 'is this mail really from who it says?'. That holds on a `full: false` fetch too — the metadata request asks for `Authentication-Results` by name, so checking whether a mail is really from who it says never costs a body. Read `dmarc` first: it is the only one of the three that ties a passing check to the visible `From` domain, so `spf: pass` alone proves nothing about the sender the user sees (a lookalike domain gets that trivially). `signedBy`/`mailedBy`/`headerFrom` name the domains each check actually validated. They do NOT have to match each other or the `From` address, and a mismatch is not by itself suspicious: a forwarded message legitimately shows the forwarder in `mailedBy` (the envelope sender is rewritten in transit) and in `signedBy` (the forwarder signs with its own key), while only `headerFrom` still names the original sender — which is exactly why `dmarc` is the result that carries meaning. Read those three as the explanation of a result, not as a test of their own. `dkimAligned` says whether a passing DKIM signature belongs to the `From` domain or a parent or child of it; it is absent when that cannot be told without a public-suffix list (two sibling subdomains), so a missing field is not a mismatch. `authservId` says WHO asserts all this: a message can carry forged Authentication-Results headers of its own, and only Gmail's own report (`mx.google.com`) is ever read; `otherReports` counts the reports that were NOT read, and `alsoReported` lists results that disagree with the ones above. `unchecked: true` means the message carried no report from Gmail — that is 'nobody looked', NOT 'nothing wrong'; unauthenticated does not imply forged, and authenticated does not imply honest (a phisher can hold a passing DMARC on his own lookalike domain). USE WHEN: reading a thread's content after finding it via search. DO NOT USE: with a message ID — this takes thread IDs. SIDE EFFECTS: none (does not mark as read).
name: get_thread
